b: Phuong Mai Nguyen’s In Waves, an adaptation of AJ Dungo’s graphic memoir of the same name, opens with Native Hawaiians performing a ritual out on the ocean, animated in a style that recalls kākau, the traditional Hawaiian art of tattooing. The film is dotted with such allegorical asides, which trace the history of surfing as a spiritual communion with the sea. They rhyme with the way that AJ (voiced in the English-language version by Will Sharpe) and his ailing girlfriend, Kristen (Stephanie Hsu), keep returning to the water to reconnect with their friends, their families, and, ultimately, the very act of living.

The story is told through the eyes of an older AJ, who’s been holed up in a van near the beach, drawing on his memories to, well, draw his memories. Nguyen and the film’s team of animators render those recollections in a dreamy watercolor style that makes even the scenes set on dry land feel as if the sea itself were conjuring a love story out of waves and whirlpools.

Anyone hoping that In Waves will follow those two distinctive threads to a satisfying conclusion, however, may be disappointed to find that the film settles into a fairly standard boy-meets-sick-girl story. AJ, a shy artist, meets Kristen, a free-spirited surfer, in high school, and over the course of their young romance, she teaches him to appreciate the ocean that’s been practically in his backyard his whole life. Meanwhile, AJ’s talent and his clear love of drawing point him toward a gleaming future in art school and, possibly, a big gig in New York.

The trouble starts before either of their lives can shift into gear. Kristen is diagnosed with cancer early on, and the disease hangs over the star-crossed couple from then on. The film hits most of the familiar beats of dramas about young love in the shadow of serious illness, but to its credit, it puts more weight on defying the illness than on its effects. Its strength lies in the couple’s outlook: riding the wave, as AJ puts it, rather than fixating on the moment they wipe out.

There’s joy and humor here, and a healthy respect for surfing as a spiritual practice, even if the film offers nowhere near enough of the history it teases. All of it is buoyed by AJ and Kristen, genuinely good people whose warm presences light up the screen. So even as it skims the surface of a more distinctive telling, it’s hard to knock In Waves too much for being what it is. For all its visual audacity, it’s a simple story, told honestly, that plays like a tapestry of abstract memories. There’s power in the telling, even if it’s a tale you’ve probably heard before.
